PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Area is the amount of surface a shape covers. In this sub-strand you will compare surfaces by placing one on the other, cover squares and rectangles with unit squares, and find area by multiplying the number of rows by the number of columns.

## Strand 2.0: Measurement
Sub-strand 2.2: Area
Suggested lessons: 8

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) compare the area of given surfaces by direct manipulation
b) calculate the area of squares and rectangles by counting unit squares
c) calculate the area of squares and rectangles as a product of number of rows and columns
d) appreciate the use of rows and columns in calculating the area of squares and rectangles in real-life situations

## What this sub-strand covers
• Area of squares and triangles

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can you work out area of different surfaces?

## Core competencies
• Critical thinking and problem solving: learner works independently to calculate the area of squares and rectangles by multiplying number of rows by the number of columns.
• Digital literacy: learner teams up with others to play games involving the areas of rectangles and squares using digital resources.

## Values
• Unity: learner works with peers harmoniously to establish that the area of a rectangle or a square is the same as the number of rows multiplied by the number of columns.
• Integrity: learner gives honest answers while counting the number of unit square cut-outs used to cover the surface.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Environmental Education: learner counts the number of unit square cut-outs prepared from locally available materials to cover the surface.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate counting of the number of unit square cut-outs prepared from locally available resources to properties of matter in Science and Technology.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Mathematics Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Measurement, Sub-strand 2.2 Area
• KICD Grade 4 Mathematics radio lesson: Area of regular shapes

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Comparing areas by placing surfaces

LESSON 1: COMPARING AREAS BY PLACING SURFACES
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain area as the amount of surface covered.
• Compare two surfaces by placing one on the other.

Curriculum outcomes: a) compare the area of given surfaces by direct manipulation

## Introduction
Two mats can look similar until you lay one on top of the other. The mat that still sticks out covers more surface. That amount of surface is called area.

## Notes
Area is the size of a surface. A book cover, a desk top, a window pane and a floor all have area. A bigger surface has a bigger area.

### Direct comparison
The surest way to compare two flat surfaces is to place one on the other, with their edges lined up as well as you can.

- If one surface sticks out all the way around, it has the larger area.
- If each surface sticks out in a different place, look at which leftover part is bigger. You may need to cover them with the same small squares before you decide.
- If the edges match exactly, the areas are equal.

Looking from a distance can trick you. A long thin strip and a square may cover the same amount of surface even though their shapes are different.

### Squares, rectangles and other shapes
A square has four equal sides and four square corners. A rectangle has opposite sides equal and four square corners. A triangle has three sides. You can still compare a triangle with a square by placing one on the other. The shape that leaves part of the other uncovered, and is not itself covered, needs a second look: covering both with the same unit squares is the fair test you will use in the next lesson.

### What this comparison does not tell you
Placing surfaces tells you which area is larger. It does not yet tell you the number of the area. To get a number, you cover the surface with equal unit squares and count them.

## Key words
• area — the amount of surface a shape or object covers
• surface — the flat face of an object, such as the top of a desk

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A slate is placed on an exercise book. The book sticks out on every side. Which has the larger area?

Working:
1. The book is not completely covered by the slate.
2. The part that sticks out is extra surface, so the book covers more.

Answer: The exercise book

### Example 2
Surface A is covered by 20 equal unit squares. Surface B is covered by 15 of the same squares. Which area is larger, and by how many unit squares?

Working:
1. 20 is more than 15.
2. 20 − 15 = 5.

Answer: Surface A is larger by 5 unit squares.

## Activity: Which surface is bigger?
You will need: Two books of different sizes, A sheet of paper, A leaf or a cut-out triangle, Scissors if an adult is present
1. Work with a partner. Place the smaller book on the larger book and say which has the greater area.
2. Place a sheet of paper on the desk. Does the paper cover the whole desk top?
3. Cut or tear a paper square and a paper triangle. Place one on the other and discuss which covers more surface.
4. Find two surfaces in the classroom that look different but might have nearly the same area. Explain how you would check.

## Practice
1. A handkerchief is placed on a face towel. The towel sticks out on all sides. Which has the larger area?
2. Two cards match exactly when one is placed on the other. What can you say about their areas?
3. Mat A is covered by 28 equal squares and mat B by 31 of the same squares. Which mat has the larger area, and by how many squares?

## Summary
• Area is the amount of surface covered.
• Place one surface on the other to see which area is larger.
• Equal edges mean equal areas. A number for the area comes from covering with unit squares.

### Answers to practice
1. The face towel
2. The areas are equal.
3. Mat B is larger by 3 squares.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Covering a surface with unit squares

LESSON 2: COVERING A SURFACE WITH UNIT SQUARES
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Cover a square or a rectangle with unit squares without gaps or overlaps.
• State that the area is the number of unit squares used.

Curriculum outcomes: b) calculate the area of squares and rectangles by counting unit squares

## Introduction
If you tile a floor, every tile is the same size and the tiles meet without leaving holes. Counting those tiles gives the area of the floor. One tile stands for one unit square.

## Notes
A unit square is a square used as the measuring piece for area. In class it may be a cut-out of side 1 cm, a bottle top arranged in a square, or a square drawn in your book. The same unit must be used for the whole surface.

### Covering without gaps or overlaps
The unit squares must:

- cover the surface completely,
- not overlap,
- not hang off the edge.

If squares overlap, you count some surface twice and the area looks too big. If there are gaps, some surface is missed and the area looks too small.

The area is the number of unit squares that cover the surface. A rectangle covered by 24 unit squares has an area of 24 unit squares.

### Squares and rectangles
On a square, the same number of unit squares fits along each side. On a rectangle, the number along the length can be different from the number along the width.

A square that holds 5 unit squares along each side is covered by 5 rows with 5 squares in each row. A rectangle might hold 6 along the length and 4 along the width.

### Say which unit you used
Twenty small squares and twenty large squares do not cover the same surface. Always name the unit: 20 one-centimetre squares, or 20 tiles of the size you used. Cut-outs from old cardboard or thick paper work well, and they use material that might otherwise be thrown away.

## Key words
• unit square — one equal square used to cover a surface when measuring area
• cover — to lay unit squares over a surface with no gaps and no overlaps

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A rectangle is covered by 4 rows with 6 unit squares in each row. What is its area?

Working:
1. Count the squares: 4 rows of 6.
2. 4 × 6 = 24 unit squares.

Answer: 24 unit squares

### Example 2
A square is covered by 5 rows with 5 unit squares in each row. What is its area?

Working:
1. 5 × 5 = 25.

Answer: 25 unit squares

## Activity: Cover the shape
You will need: Cardboard or paper cut into equal squares, A rectangular piece of paper, Pencil
1. In a group, cut equal unit squares from used cardboard or thick paper.
2. Cover a rectangular sheet completely. Do not leave gaps and do not overlap the squares.
3. Count the unit squares and write the area.
4. Cover a square sheet with the same unit squares and write that area too.
5. Compare your counts with another group. If the numbers differ, check for gaps or overlaps.

## Practice
1. A card is covered by 3 rows of 8 unit squares. What is its area?
2. Why must the unit squares not overlap?
3. A square stamp picture is covered by 4 rows of 4 unit squares. What is its area?

## Summary
• Cover the surface with equal unit squares, with no gaps and no overlaps.
• The area is the number of unit squares used.
• Name the unit, because different squares cover different amounts of surface.

### Answers to practice
1. 24 unit squares
2. Overlapping counts some of the surface more than once, so the area would be too big.
3. 16 unit squares

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Counting unit squares

LESSON 3: COUNTING UNIT SQUARES
===============================

## What you will learn
• Count unit squares row by row on a square and on a rectangle.
• Give an honest count of the squares that cover a surface.

Curriculum outcomes: b) calculate the area of squares and rectangles by counting unit squares

## Introduction
A shopkeeper who counts tiles twice will order too many. A careful count, row by row, gives the true area of a square or a rectangle.

## Notes
When the unit squares are already drawn, you do not need to cut new ones. You count the squares that are there.

### Count one row, then the rows
Touch each square in the first row and write how many there are. Check that every other full row has the same number. Then count the rows.

Area = squares in one row × number of rows.

You can also add. A rectangle with 3 rows of 7 squares has area 7 + 7 + 7 = 21 unit squares. Multiplication is the short way of doing that addition.

### Do not count lines
The grid lines are the edges of the squares. Count the squares themselves, not the lines. A row with 6 squares has 7 lines if you count both ends, and that 7 is not the area.

### Squares
On a square, the number of squares in a row equals the number of rows. Four rows of 4 give 16. Six rows of 6 give 36. Nine rows of 9 give 81.

### An honest count
If you lose your place, start the row again. Do not guess the last few squares. Two learners should be allowed to get the same number when they cover the same surface with the same unit squares. Writing a larger number to finish quickly is not correct measuring.

## Key words
• row — a line of unit squares going across
• grid — unit squares drawn in rows and columns

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A rectangle has 7 rows with 3 unit squares in each row. Find the area by addition and by multiplication.

Working:
1. Addition: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 21.
2. Multiplication: 7 × 3 = 21.

Answer: 21 unit squares

### Example 2
A square grid has 8 unit squares along each side. What is its area?

Working:
1. The square has 8 rows of 8.
2. 8 × 8 = 64.

Answer: 64 unit squares

## Activity: Count every square
You will need: Squared paper or a grid drawn on manila paper, Pencil, Small stones or seeds as counters
1. Draw a rectangle 6 squares long and 4 squares wide on squared paper.
2. Put a seed on each square as you count, so that you do not count any square twice.
3. Write the area. Ask a partner to count the same rectangle without looking at your number.
4. Draw a square of side 5 unit squares and count its area in the same way.
5. If your two counts differ, recount together until you agree.

## Practice
1. How many unit squares cover a rectangle that is 9 squares long and 2 squares wide?
2. A square has 6 unit squares along each side. What is its area?
3. A learner counts the lines along one side of a grid and gets 5. There are 4 unit squares in that row. What should be recorded as the number in the row?

## Summary
• Count squares, not the grid lines.
• Squares in one row times the number of rows gives the area.
• The same surface and the same unit squares must give the same count.

### Answers to practice
1. 18 unit squares
2. 36 unit squares
3. 4 unit squares

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Area as rows multiplied by columns

LESSON 4: AREA AS ROWS MULTIPLIED BY COLUMNS
============================================

## What you will learn
• Identify rows and columns on a square or rectangle.
• Calculate the area as the number of rows multiplied by the number of columns.

Curriculum outcomes: c) calculate the area of squares and rectangles as a product of number of rows and columns

## Introduction
Counting thirty tiles one by one is slow, and it is easy to skip one. If you know there are 5 rows and 6 columns, one multiplication gives the same area.

## Notes
A row runs across. A column runs from top to bottom. On a rectangle of unit squares, every row has the same number of squares, and every column has the same number of squares.

### The rule
Area of a rectangle or a square = number of rows × number of columns.

The order does not change the answer. Six rows of 4 columns and 4 rows of 6 columns both cover 24 unit squares. The shapes may face different ways, but the areas are equal.

### A square
In a square, the number of rows equals the number of columns. A square with 9 rows has 9 columns, so the area is 9 × 9 = 81 unit squares.

### Matching the count
Rows × columns must agree with counting. Three rows and 5 columns:

- Row by row: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15.
- Multiplication: 3 × 5 = 15.

If the two answers differ, check whether you counted a row twice or multiplied the wrong numbers.

### Units
The answer is a number of unit squares. If each unit square is a floor tile, the area is that many tiles. If each unit square measures 1 cm along each side, the area is that many square centimetres. Keep the unit in the answer.

## Key words
• column — a line of unit squares going from top to bottom
• square centimetre — the area of a unit square that measures 1 cm along each side

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A rectangle has 8 rows and 5 columns of unit squares. Find its area.

Working:
1. Area = rows × columns.
2. 8 × 5 = 40.

Answer: 40 unit squares

### Example 2
A square tile pattern has 9 rows. How many unit squares is that?

Working:
1. A square has the same number of columns as rows.
2. 9 × 9 = 81.

Answer: 81 unit squares

### Example 3
Show that 6 rows of 4 columns cover the same area as 4 rows of 6 columns.

Working:
1. 6 × 4 = 24.
2. 4 × 6 = 24.

Answer: Both cover 24 unit squares.

## Activity: Rows times columns
You will need: Squared paper, Pencil, Bottle tops or seeds
1. With a partner, build a rectangle using 4 rows of 6 seeds.
2. Write rows × columns and find the area. Then count the seeds to check.
3. Rearrange the same seeds into 6 rows of 4. Work out the area again.
4. Build a square with 5 rows and 5 columns and record its area.
5. Explain to another pair why multiplying is quicker than counting every seed on a large rectangle.

## Practice
1. Find the area of a rectangle with 7 rows and 6 columns of unit squares.
2. A square has 10 rows of unit squares. What is its area?
3. A card has 3 rows and 11 columns. What is its area?
4. Which has the larger area: 5 rows by 8 columns, or 6 rows by 7 columns? By how many unit squares?

## Summary
• Area = number of rows × number of columns.
• On a square, the number of rows equals the number of columns.
• Changing the order of the two numbers does not change the area.

### Answers to practice
1. 42 unit squares
2. 100 unit squares
3. 33 unit squares
4. 6 by 7 is larger by 2 unit squares.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: Area of tiled floors

LESSON 5: AREA OF TILED FLOORS
==============================

## What you will learn
• Find the number of tiles on a rectangular or square floor.
• Find how many whole tiles remain when some are broken or missing.

Curriculum outcomes: c) calculate the area of squares and rectangles as a product of number of rows and columns; d) appreciate the use of rows and columns in calculating the area of squares and rectangles in real-life situations

## Introduction
A veranda, a classroom floor or a paved path is often covered with tiles of the same size. The number of tiles is the area of that floor in tile units.

## Notes
Stand at one corner of a tiled rectangle. Count the tiles in one row. That number is the number of columns. Then count how many such rows there are.

Area in tiles = rows × columns.

A veranda with 4 rows of 12 tiles has 4 × 12 = 48 tiles. A square courtyard with 11 tiles along each side has 11 × 11 = 121 tiles.

### Broken or missing tiles
If some tiles are cracked, first find how many tiles the whole rectangle would have. Then subtract the broken ones.

A floor of 7 rows and 8 columns has 56 tiles. If 5 are broken, the whole tiles left are 56 − 5 = 51.

### Comparing two floors
Work out each area, then subtract. A room of 6 rows and 9 columns has 54 tiles. A room of 8 rows and 7 columns has 56 tiles. The second room has 56 − 54 = 2 tiles more area.

### Why rows and columns help
On a large paved floor you cannot pick up the tiles to count them in your hands. Multiplying rows by columns gives the area while the tiles stay in place. It is the same number you would get by counting every tile, if the rows are equal and you do not skip one.

## Key words
• tile — one of the equal pieces that cover a floor; here it is used as a unit square
• paved — covered with flat stones or tiles

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A veranda has 4 rows of 12 tiles. How many tiles cover it?

Working:
1. Area = rows × columns.
2. 4 × 12 = 48.

Answer: 48 tiles

### Example 2
A floor has 7 rows and 8 columns of tiles. Five tiles are broken. How many tiles are still whole?

Working:
1. Whole floor: 7 × 8 = 56 tiles.
2. 56 − 5 = 51.

Answer: 51 tiles

### Example 3
Room A has 6 rows of 9 tiles. Room B has 8 rows of 7 tiles. Which floor has the larger area, and by how many tiles?

Working:
1. Room A: 6 × 9 = 54.
2. Room B: 8 × 7 = 56.
3. 56 − 54 = 2.

Answer: Room B is larger by 2 tiles.

## Activity: Tiles on the floor
You will need: A tiled or paved floor, or a grid drawn with chalk, Exercise book
1. In a group, find a rectangular tiled space, or draw a rectangle of equal squares with chalk.
2. Count the tiles in one row and the number of rows.
3. Multiply to find the area. Two people should multiply separately and compare answers.
4. Imagine 3 tiles are broken. Work out how many whole tiles would remain.
5. Talk about another place, such as a path or a courtyard, where rows and columns would help you find the area.

## Practice
1. A path has 2 rows of 15 paving tiles. How many tiles is that?
2. A square floor has 12 tiles along each side. What is its area in tiles?
3. A room has 9 rows of 6 tiles, and 8 tiles are missing. How many tiles are in place?
4. Why is rows × columns useful on a floor you cannot pick up?

## Summary
• On a tiled rectangle, area in tiles = rows × columns.
• Subtract broken or missing tiles from the full area.
• Compare two floors by working out both areas and subtracting.

### Answers to practice
1. 30 tiles
2. 144 tiles
3. 46 tiles
4. You can find the number of tiles while they stay in place, without counting every tile one by one.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Choosing how to find an area

LESSON 6: CHOOSING HOW TO FIND AN AREA
======================================

## What you will learn
• Decide whether to compare surfaces, count unit squares, or multiply rows by columns.
• Explain why rows and columns are useful in real measuring.

Curriculum outcomes: a) compare the area of given surfaces by direct manipulation; d) appreciate the use of rows and columns in calculating the area of squares and rectangles in real-life situations

## Introduction
You now have three ways to work with area. Placing one surface on another shows which is bigger. Counting unit squares gives a number. Multiplying rows by columns gives that number quickly when the rows are equal.

## Notes
Choose the method that matches the question.

### Which surface is bigger?
If you only need to compare, place one surface on the other. A triangle and a square can be compared in this way. You do not have to multiply unless you need the number of unit squares.

### How many unit squares?
If the surface is covered, or can be covered, with equal squares, the area is the number of those squares. Count them when there are only a few. If you see equal rows and columns, multiply.

### Check a multiplication by counting
A small rectangle of 4 rows and 3 columns has area 12. Counting all 12 squares checks the multiplication. On a large floor, check by multiplying in the other order: 4 × 3 and 3 × 4 should match. You can also add the rows: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.

### Where people use this
Builders count tiles before they pave a floor. A person laying a mat wants a mat that covers the sleeping space. Farmers look at which plot of ground covers more land before they decide where to plant. In each case the fair comparison uses the same unit.

Giving the true count matters. If a group reports 40 squares but only 36 were used, the area is wrong and a buyer might order the wrong number of tiles.

## Key words
• compare — to decide which of two areas is larger or whether they are equal
• check — a second method that should give the same area

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A square has 4 rows and 4 columns of tiles. A rectangle has 2 rows and 8 columns. Compare their areas.

Working:
1. Square: 4 × 4 = 16.
2. Rectangle: 2 × 8 = 16.
3. The areas are equal.

Answer: Both have an area of 16 tiles.

### Example 2
A small rectangle is said to have area 5 × 4 = 20 unit squares. Check by addition of the rows.

Working:
1. Five rows of 4: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4.
2. 4 × 5 = 20, so the multiplication agrees.

Answer: 20 unit squares

## Activity: Area game
You will need: Number cards for rows and columns, Squared paper, Pencil
1. In pairs, draw two cards, one for the number of rows and one for the number of columns. Use numbers from 2 to 10.
2. Each person multiplies to find the area. If you agree, sketch the rectangle on squared paper and count to check.
3. Score a point for a correct area. Play five rounds.
4. For one round, also place two paper rectangles on each other and say which looks larger before you calculate.
5. If you have a digital device and your teacher allows it, play a tile-covering game and record one area you found.

## Practice
1. When is placing one surface on the other enough, without counting?
2. A learner says 7 rows of 8 columns make 56 unit squares. Check using 8 × 7.
3. A cloth is 10 rows by 10 columns of unit squares. Another is 12 rows by 8 columns. Which area is larger, and by how many unit squares?

## Summary
• Compare by placing surfaces when you only need to know which is larger.
• Count unit squares, or multiply rows by columns, when you need the number.
• Check a large area by multiplying in the other order or by adding one row several times.

### Answers to practice
1. When you only need to know which surface has the larger area, or whether the areas are equal.
2. 56 unit squares
3. The cloth of 10 by 10 is larger by 4 unit squares.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 2.2 AREA
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. A small mat is placed on a large mat. The large mat sticks out on every side. Which has the greater area?
   A. The small mat
   B. The large mat
   C. They have the same area

2. Surface A is covered by 18 of the same unit squares and surface B by 23. How many more unit squares does B have?

3. A rectangle is covered by 6 rows of 4 unit squares. What is its area?
   A. 10 unit squares
   B. 24 unit squares
   C. 20 unit squares
   D. 64 unit squares

4. A square is covered by 7 rows of 7 unit squares. What is its area?

5. What must you avoid when covering a surface with unit squares?
   A. Using equal squares
   B. Leaving gaps or overlapping the squares
   C. Counting every square

6. A rectangle has 9 rows and 3 columns of unit squares. What is its area?
   A. 12 unit squares
   B. 27 unit squares
   C. 93 unit squares
   D. 6 unit squares

7. A paved floor has 8 rows of 11 tiles. How many tiles cover it?

8. A floor of 5 rows and 6 columns has 4 broken tiles. How many tiles are still whole?

9. A square has 4 rows of tiles and a rectangle has 2 rows of 8 tiles. Which statement is true?
   A. The square is larger by 8 tiles
   B. The rectangle is larger by 8 tiles
   C. The areas are equal

10. Why do we multiply the number of rows by the number of columns on a large tiled floor?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 2.2 AREA
========================================

1. B. The large mat
   The surface that sticks out covers more, so the large mat has the greater area.

2. 5
   23 − 18 = 5.

3. B. 24 unit squares
   6 × 4 = 24 unit squares.

4. 49 unit squares
   7 × 7 = 49.

5. B. Leaving gaps or overlapping the squares
   Gaps miss some surface and overlaps count some surface twice.

6. B. 27 unit squares
   Area = rows × columns = 9 × 3 = 27.

7. 88 tiles
   8 × 11 = 88.

8. 26 tiles
   5 × 6 = 30, then 30 − 4 = 26.

9. C. The areas are equal
   4 × 4 = 16 and 2 × 8 = 16.

10. It gives the number of tiles quickly, without counting every tile and losing the count.
   Rows × columns equals the count of the unit squares when every row is full.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Area is the amount of surface a shape covers. In this sub-strand you will compare surfaces by placing one on the other, cover squares and rectangles with unit squares, and find area by multiplying the number of rows by the number of columns.

## Strand 2.0: Measurement
Sub-strand 2.2: Area
Suggested lessons: 8

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) compare the area of given surfaces by direct manipulation
b) calculate the area of squares and rectangles by counting unit squares
c) calculate the area of squares and rectangles as a product of number of rows and columns
d) appreciate the use of rows and columns in calculating the area of squares and rectangles in real-life situations

## What this sub-strand covers
• Area of squares and triangles

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can you work out area of different surfaces?

## Core competencies
• Critical thinking and problem solving: learner works independently to calculate the area of squares and rectangles by multiplying number of rows by the number of columns.
• Digital literacy: learner teams up with others to play games involving the areas of rectangles and squares using digital resources.

## Values
• Unity: learner works with peers harmoniously to establish that the area of a rectangle or a square is the same as the number of rows multiplied by the number of columns.
• Integrity: learner gives honest answers while counting the number of unit square cut-outs used to cover the surface.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Environmental Education: learner counts the number of unit square cut-outs prepared from locally available materials to cover the surface.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate counting of the number of unit square cut-outs prepared from locally available resources to properties of matter in Science and Technology.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Mathematics Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Measurement, Sub-strand 2.2 Area
• KICD Grade 4 Mathematics radio lesson: Area of regular shapes

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Comparing areas by placing surfaces
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: COMPARING AREAS BY PLACING SURFACES
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain area as the amount of surface covered.
• Compare two surfaces by placing one on the other.

Curriculum outcomes: a) compare the area of given surfaces by direct manipulation

## Introduction
Two mats can look similar until you lay one on top of the other. The mat that still sticks out covers more surface. That amount of surface is called area.

## Notes
Area is the size of a surface. A book cover, a desk top, a window pane and a floor all have area. A bigger surface has a bigger area.

### Direct comparison
The surest way to compare two flat surfaces is to place one on the other, with their edges lined up as well as you can.

- If one surface sticks out all the way around, it has the larger area.
- If each surface sticks out in a different place, look at which leftover part is bigger. You may need to cover them with the same small squares before you decide.
- If the edges match exactly, the areas are equal.

Looking from a distance can trick you. A long thin strip and a square may cover the same amount of surface even though their shapes are different.

### Squares, rectangles and other shapes
A square has four equal sides and four square corners. A rectangle has opposite sides equal and four square corners. A triangle has three sides. You can still compare a triangle with a square by placing one on the other. The shape that leaves part of the other uncovered, and is not itself covered, needs a second look: covering both with the same unit squares is the fair test you will use in the next lesson.

### What this comparison does not tell you
Placing surfaces tells you which area is larger. It does not yet tell you the number of the area. To get a number, you cover the surface with equal unit squares and count them.

## Key words
• area — the amount of surface a shape or object covers
• surface — the flat face of an object, such as the top of a desk

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A slate is placed on an exercise book. The book sticks out on every side. Which has the larger area?

Working:
1. The book is not completely covered by the slate.
2. The part that sticks out is extra surface, so the book covers more.

Answer: The exercise book

### Example 2
Surface A is covered by 20 equal unit squares. Surface B is covered by 15 of the same squares. Which area is larger, and by how many unit squares?

Working:
1. 20 is more than 15.
2. 20 − 15 = 5.

Answer: Surface A is larger by 5 unit squares.

## Activity: Which surface is bigger?
You will need: Two books of different sizes, A sheet of paper, A leaf or a cut-out triangle, Scissors if an adult is present
1. Work with a partner. Place the smaller book on the larger book and say which has the greater area.
2. Place a sheet of paper on the desk. Does the paper cover the whole desk top?
3. Cut or tear a paper square and a paper triangle. Place one on the other and discuss which covers more surface.
4. Find two surfaces in the classroom that look different but might have nearly the same area. Explain how you would check.

## Practice
1. A handkerchief is placed on a face towel. The towel sticks out on all sides. Which has the larger area?
2. Two cards match exactly when one is placed on the other. What can you say about their areas?
3. Mat A is covered by 28 equal squares and mat B by 31 of the same squares. Which mat has the larger area, and by how many squares?

## Summary
• Area is the amount of surface covered.
• Place one surface on the other to see which area is larger.
• Equal edges mean equal areas. A number for the area comes from covering with unit squares.

### Answers to practice
1. The face towel
2. The areas are equal.
3. Mat B is larger by 3 squares.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Covering a surface with unit squares
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: COVERING A SURFACE WITH UNIT SQUARES
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Cover a square or a rectangle with unit squares without gaps or overlaps.
• State that the area is the number of unit squares used.

Curriculum outcomes: b) calculate the area of squares and rectangles by counting unit squares

## Introduction
If you tile a floor, every tile is the same size and the tiles meet without leaving holes. Counting those tiles gives the area of the floor. One tile stands for one unit square.

## Notes
A unit square is a square used as the measuring piece for area. In class it may be a cut-out of side 1 cm, a bottle top arranged in a square, or a square drawn in your book. The same unit must be used for the whole surface.

### Covering without gaps or overlaps
The unit squares must:

- cover the surface completely,
- not overlap,
- not hang off the edge.

If squares overlap, you count some surface twice and the area looks too big. If there are gaps, some surface is missed and the area looks too small.

The area is the number of unit squares that cover the surface. A rectangle covered by 24 unit squares has an area of 24 unit squares.

### Squares and rectangles
On a square, the same number of unit squares fits along each side. On a rectangle, the number along the length can be different from the number along the width.

A square that holds 5 unit squares along each side is covered by 5 rows with 5 squares in each row. A rectangle might hold 6 along the length and 4 along the width.

### Say which unit you used
Twenty small squares and twenty large squares do not cover the same surface. Always name the unit: 20 one-centimetre squares, or 20 tiles of the size you used. Cut-outs from old cardboard or thick paper work well, and they use material that might otherwise be thrown away.

## Key words
• unit square — one equal square used to cover a surface when measuring area
• cover — to lay unit squares over a surface with no gaps and no overlaps

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A rectangle is covered by 4 rows with 6 unit squares in each row. What is its area?

Working:
1. Count the squares: 4 rows of 6.
2. 4 × 6 = 24 unit squares.

Answer: 24 unit squares

### Example 2
A square is covered by 5 rows with 5 unit squares in each row. What is its area?

Working:
1. 5 × 5 = 25.

Answer: 25 unit squares

## Activity: Cover the shape
You will need: Cardboard or paper cut into equal squares, A rectangular piece of paper, Pencil
1. In a group, cut equal unit squares from used cardboard or thick paper.
2. Cover a rectangular sheet completely. Do not leave gaps and do not overlap the squares.
3. Count the unit squares and write the area.
4. Cover a square sheet with the same unit squares and write that area too.
5. Compare your counts with another group. If the numbers differ, check for gaps or overlaps.

## Practice
1. A card is covered by 3 rows of 8 unit squares. What is its area?
2. Why must the unit squares not overlap?
3. A square stamp picture is covered by 4 rows of 4 unit squares. What is its area?

## Summary
• Cover the surface with equal unit squares, with no gaps and no overlaps.
• The area is the number of unit squares used.
• Name the unit, because different squares cover different amounts of surface.

### Answers to practice
1. 24 unit squares
2. Overlapping counts some of the surface more than once, so the area would be too big.
3. 16 unit squares

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Counting unit squares
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: COUNTING UNIT SQUARES
===============================

## What you will learn
• Count unit squares row by row on a square and on a rectangle.
• Give an honest count of the squares that cover a surface.

Curriculum outcomes: b) calculate the area of squares and rectangles by counting unit squares

## Introduction
A shopkeeper who counts tiles twice will order too many. A careful count, row by row, gives the true area of a square or a rectangle.

## Notes
When the unit squares are already drawn, you do not need to cut new ones. You count the squares that are there.

### Count one row, then the rows
Touch each square in the first row and write how many there are. Check that every other full row has the same number. Then count the rows.

Area = squares in one row × number of rows.

You can also add. A rectangle with 3 rows of 7 squares has area 7 + 7 + 7 = 21 unit squares. Multiplication is the short way of doing that addition.

### Do not count lines
The grid lines are the edges of the squares. Count the squares themselves, not the lines. A row with 6 squares has 7 lines if you count both ends, and that 7 is not the area.

### Squares
On a square, the number of squares in a row equals the number of rows. Four rows of 4 give 16. Six rows of 6 give 36. Nine rows of 9 give 81.

### An honest count
If you lose your place, start the row again. Do not guess the last few squares. Two learners should be allowed to get the same number when they cover the same surface with the same unit squares. Writing a larger number to finish quickly is not correct measuring.

## Key words
• row — a line of unit squares going across
• grid — unit squares drawn in rows and columns

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A rectangle has 7 rows with 3 unit squares in each row. Find the area by addition and by multiplication.

Working:
1. Addition: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 21.
2. Multiplication: 7 × 3 = 21.

Answer: 21 unit squares

### Example 2
A square grid has 8 unit squares along each side. What is its area?

Working:
1. The square has 8 rows of 8.
2. 8 × 8 = 64.

Answer: 64 unit squares

## Activity: Count every square
You will need: Squared paper or a grid drawn on manila paper, Pencil, Small stones or seeds as counters
1. Draw a rectangle 6 squares long and 4 squares wide on squared paper.
2. Put a seed on each square as you count, so that you do not count any square twice.
3. Write the area. Ask a partner to count the same rectangle without looking at your number.
4. Draw a square of side 5 unit squares and count its area in the same way.
5. If your two counts differ, recount together until you agree.

## Practice
1. How many unit squares cover a rectangle that is 9 squares long and 2 squares wide?
2. A square has 6 unit squares along each side. What is its area?
3. A learner counts the lines along one side of a grid and gets 5. There are 4 unit squares in that row. What should be recorded as the number in the row?

## Summary
• Count squares, not the grid lines.
• Squares in one row times the number of rows gives the area.
• The same surface and the same unit squares must give the same count.

### Answers to practice
1. 18 unit squares
2. 36 unit squares
3. 4 unit squares

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Area as rows multiplied by columns
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: AREA AS ROWS MULTIPLIED BY COLUMNS
============================================

## What you will learn
• Identify rows and columns on a square or rectangle.
• Calculate the area as the number of rows multiplied by the number of columns.

Curriculum outcomes: c) calculate the area of squares and rectangles as a product of number of rows and columns

## Introduction
Counting thirty tiles one by one is slow, and it is easy to skip one. If you know there are 5 rows and 6 columns, one multiplication gives the same area.

## Notes
A row runs across. A column runs from top to bottom. On a rectangle of unit squares, every row has the same number of squares, and every column has the same number of squares.

### The rule
Area of a rectangle or a square = number of rows × number of columns.

The order does not change the answer. Six rows of 4 columns and 4 rows of 6 columns both cover 24 unit squares. The shapes may face different ways, but the areas are equal.

### A square
In a square, the number of rows equals the number of columns. A square with 9 rows has 9 columns, so the area is 9 × 9 = 81 unit squares.

### Matching the count
Rows × columns must agree with counting. Three rows and 5 columns:

- Row by row: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15.
- Multiplication: 3 × 5 = 15.

If the two answers differ, check whether you counted a row twice or multiplied the wrong numbers.

### Units
The answer is a number of unit squares. If each unit square is a floor tile, the area is that many tiles. If each unit square measures 1 cm along each side, the area is that many square centimetres. Keep the unit in the answer.

## Key words
• column — a line of unit squares going from top to bottom
• square centimetre — the area of a unit square that measures 1 cm along each side

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A rectangle has 8 rows and 5 columns of unit squares. Find its area.

Working:
1. Area = rows × columns.
2. 8 × 5 = 40.

Answer: 40 unit squares

### Example 2
A square tile pattern has 9 rows. How many unit squares is that?

Working:
1. A square has the same number of columns as rows.
2. 9 × 9 = 81.

Answer: 81 unit squares

### Example 3
Show that 6 rows of 4 columns cover the same area as 4 rows of 6 columns.

Working:
1. 6 × 4 = 24.
2. 4 × 6 = 24.

Answer: Both cover 24 unit squares.

## Activity: Rows times columns
You will need: Squared paper, Pencil, Bottle tops or seeds
1. With a partner, build a rectangle using 4 rows of 6 seeds.
2. Write rows × columns and find the area. Then count the seeds to check.
3. Rearrange the same seeds into 6 rows of 4. Work out the area again.
4. Build a square with 5 rows and 5 columns and record its area.
5. Explain to another pair why multiplying is quicker than counting every seed on a large rectangle.

## Practice
1. Find the area of a rectangle with 7 rows and 6 columns of unit squares.
2. A square has 10 rows of unit squares. What is its area?
3. A card has 3 rows and 11 columns. What is its area?
4. Which has the larger area: 5 rows by 8 columns, or 6 rows by 7 columns? By how many unit squares?

## Summary
• Area = number of rows × number of columns.
• On a square, the number of rows equals the number of columns.
• Changing the order of the two numbers does not change the area.

### Answers to practice
1. 42 unit squares
2. 100 unit squares
3. 33 unit squares
4. 6 by 7 is larger by 2 unit squares.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Area of tiled floors
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: AREA OF TILED FLOORS
==============================

## What you will learn
• Find the number of tiles on a rectangular or square floor.
• Find how many whole tiles remain when some are broken or missing.

Curriculum outcomes: c) calculate the area of squares and rectangles as a product of number of rows and columns; d) appreciate the use of rows and columns in calculating the area of squares and rectangles in real-life situations

## Introduction
A veranda, a classroom floor or a paved path is often covered with tiles of the same size. The number of tiles is the area of that floor in tile units.

## Notes
Stand at one corner of a tiled rectangle. Count the tiles in one row. That number is the number of columns. Then count how many such rows there are.

Area in tiles = rows × columns.

A veranda with 4 rows of 12 tiles has 4 × 12 = 48 tiles. A square courtyard with 11 tiles along each side has 11 × 11 = 121 tiles.

### Broken or missing tiles
If some tiles are cracked, first find how many tiles the whole rectangle would have. Then subtract the broken ones.

A floor of 7 rows and 8 columns has 56 tiles. If 5 are broken, the whole tiles left are 56 − 5 = 51.

### Comparing two floors
Work out each area, then subtract. A room of 6 rows and 9 columns has 54 tiles. A room of 8 rows and 7 columns has 56 tiles. The second room has 56 − 54 = 2 tiles more area.

### Why rows and columns help
On a large paved floor you cannot pick up the tiles to count them in your hands. Multiplying rows by columns gives the area while the tiles stay in place. It is the same number you would get by counting every tile, if the rows are equal and you do not skip one.

## Key words
• tile — one of the equal pieces that cover a floor; here it is used as a unit square
• paved — covered with flat stones or tiles

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A veranda has 4 rows of 12 tiles. How many tiles cover it?

Working:
1. Area = rows × columns.
2. 4 × 12 = 48.

Answer: 48 tiles

### Example 2
A floor has 7 rows and 8 columns of tiles. Five tiles are broken. How many tiles are still whole?

Working:
1. Whole floor: 7 × 8 = 56 tiles.
2. 56 − 5 = 51.

Answer: 51 tiles

### Example 3
Room A has 6 rows of 9 tiles. Room B has 8 rows of 7 tiles. Which floor has the larger area, and by how many tiles?

Working:
1. Room A: 6 × 9 = 54.
2. Room B: 8 × 7 = 56.
3. 56 − 54 = 2.

Answer: Room B is larger by 2 tiles.

## Activity: Tiles on the floor
You will need: A tiled or paved floor, or a grid drawn with chalk, Exercise book
1. In a group, find a rectangular tiled space, or draw a rectangle of equal squares with chalk.
2. Count the tiles in one row and the number of rows.
3. Multiply to find the area. Two people should multiply separately and compare answers.
4. Imagine 3 tiles are broken. Work out how many whole tiles would remain.
5. Talk about another place, such as a path or a courtyard, where rows and columns would help you find the area.

## Practice
1. A path has 2 rows of 15 paving tiles. How many tiles is that?
2. A square floor has 12 tiles along each side. What is its area in tiles?
3. A room has 9 rows of 6 tiles, and 8 tiles are missing. How many tiles are in place?
4. Why is rows × columns useful on a floor you cannot pick up?

## Summary
• On a tiled rectangle, area in tiles = rows × columns.
• Subtract broken or missing tiles from the full area.
• Compare two floors by working out both areas and subtracting.

### Answers to practice
1. 30 tiles
2. 144 tiles
3. 46 tiles
4. You can find the number of tiles while they stay in place, without counting every tile one by one.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Choosing how to find an area
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: CHOOSING HOW TO FIND AN AREA
======================================

## What you will learn
• Decide whether to compare surfaces, count unit squares, or multiply rows by columns.
• Explain why rows and columns are useful in real measuring.

Curriculum outcomes: a) compare the area of given surfaces by direct manipulation; d) appreciate the use of rows and columns in calculating the area of squares and rectangles in real-life situations

## Introduction
You now have three ways to work with area. Placing one surface on another shows which is bigger. Counting unit squares gives a number. Multiplying rows by columns gives that number quickly when the rows are equal.

## Notes
Choose the method that matches the question.

### Which surface is bigger?
If you only need to compare, place one surface on the other. A triangle and a square can be compared in this way. You do not have to multiply unless you need the number of unit squares.

### How many unit squares?
If the surface is covered, or can be covered, with equal squares, the area is the number of those squares. Count them when there are only a few. If you see equal rows and columns, multiply.

### Check a multiplication by counting
A small rectangle of 4 rows and 3 columns has area 12. Counting all 12 squares checks the multiplication. On a large floor, check by multiplying in the other order: 4 × 3 and 3 × 4 should match. You can also add the rows: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.

### Where people use this
Builders count tiles before they pave a floor. A person laying a mat wants a mat that covers the sleeping space. Farmers look at which plot of ground covers more land before they decide where to plant. In each case the fair comparison uses the same unit.

Giving the true count matters. If a group reports 40 squares but only 36 were used, the area is wrong and a buyer might order the wrong number of tiles.

## Key words
• compare — to decide which of two areas is larger or whether they are equal
• check — a second method that should give the same area

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A square has 4 rows and 4 columns of tiles. A rectangle has 2 rows and 8 columns. Compare their areas.

Working:
1. Square: 4 × 4 = 16.
2. Rectangle: 2 × 8 = 16.
3. The areas are equal.

Answer: Both have an area of 16 tiles.

### Example 2
A small rectangle is said to have area 5 × 4 = 20 unit squares. Check by addition of the rows.

Working:
1. Five rows of 4: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4.
2. 4 × 5 = 20, so the multiplication agrees.

Answer: 20 unit squares

## Activity: Area game
You will need: Number cards for rows and columns, Squared paper, Pencil
1. In pairs, draw two cards, one for the number of rows and one for the number of columns. Use numbers from 2 to 10.
2. Each person multiplies to find the area. If you agree, sketch the rectangle on squared paper and count to check.
3. Score a point for a correct area. Play five rounds.
4. For one round, also place two paper rectangles on each other and say which looks larger before you calculate.
5. If you have a digital device and your teacher allows it, play a tile-covering game and record one area you found.

## Practice
1. When is placing one surface on the other enough, without counting?
2. A learner says 7 rows of 8 columns make 56 unit squares. Check using 8 × 7.
3. A cloth is 10 rows by 10 columns of unit squares. Another is 12 rows by 8 columns. Which area is larger, and by how many unit squares?

## Summary
• Compare by placing surfaces when you only need to know which is larger.
• Count unit squares, or multiply rows by columns, when you need the number.
• Check a large area by multiplying in the other order or by adding one row several times.

### Answers to practice
1. When you only need to know which surface has the larger area, or whether the areas are equal.
2. 56 unit squares
3. The cloth of 10 by 10 is larger by 4 unit squares.
